title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether adding a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair budget improves the probability that an intent‑driven network‑change proposal passes semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. Each pair reused the same single shared_initial LLM candidate for two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (validator + ≤1 automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10,000). The single deterministic rescue required one permitted edit. Under the supplied synthetic suite and the shared_initial estimand the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We release preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts with the run bundle to support reproducibility and targeted follow‑up studies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness (sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation) matters operationally and cannot be assured by syntactic checks alone. A common engineering pattern pairs a generative model with a deterministic validator and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. Prior work reports improvements from tool augmentation but often conflates deterministic validator effects with gains from resampling or interactive regeneration, making it difficult to bound the benefit attributable solely to post‑hoc deterministic rescue. To address this, we preregistered a paired experiment that conditions on a single LLM draw per intent (shared_initial) and measures only the deterministic verifier/repair effect when the same candidate is evaluated under two treatments.

Research question. Does integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation isolating deterministic rescue under a shared_initial estimand; (2) an artifact bundle that archives task manifests, validator traces, the single automated repair transcript, and analysis inputs; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of ceiling effects, estimator conditioning, validator coverage, and operational tradeoffs for NetOps pipelines.
sections.related_work:
LLMs and NetOps. Recent surveys and system papers document active work on intent‑driven configuration, template synthesis, automated testing, and repair in network management and communications domains [1–4]. Tool‑augmented agentic frameworks (planner‑centric and ReAct‑style pipelines) enable LLMs to call external validators, simulators, or synthesizers to coordinate multi‑step NetOps workflows; these frameworks provide architectural scaffolding for generate→validate→repair patterns [5,6].

Generate→validate→repair and verification. Empirical reports show that introducing deterministic checks and repair scaffolds can improve surface correctness relative to unconstrained generation, but effect sizes depend strongly on validator expressiveness, task distribution, and whether resampling is permitted [3,7]. Work on hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets proposes entropy‑ or semantic‑consistency detectors and retrieval augmentation to reduce false positives, but transferability to rich NetOps semantics (reachability, ordered sequences) is not fully settled [8].

Methodological gap and positioning. Many prior evaluations mix verifier effects with resampling benefits; evaluating deterministic rescue while holding a single generator draw fixed provides an operationally meaningful bound for policies that limit model calls. Our study directly addresses this methodological gap by fixing the shared_initial candidate and measuring the marginal deterministic rescue available with a constrained repair budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) with a primary estimand defined as the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 pairs. The confirmatory analysis executor and multiplicity plan were frozen before the main run. The preregistration also specified task generation, inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination controls, and a single‑call repair budget; the optional calibration pilot in the plan was not executed and the main run proceeded per the frozen plan.

Task suite and stratification. The synthetic benchmark consists of deterministically generated intents and small synthetic topologies stratified into low/medium/high difficulty according to explicit metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count). The confirmatory sample used 100 pairs per stratum.

Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic verifier/repair rescue from resampling effects we implemented a shared_initial protocol: for each pair a single LLM candidate was generated and reused verbatim for both conditions. The declared generator for the run was gpt-5-mini (as recorded in the archived model configuration). Reuse of the same candidate across conditions prevents differences due to independent additional model draws and isolates deterministic validation and the permitted bounded repair.

Deterministic validator and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic validator that implements full intent constraint validation (sequencing invariants, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants, and forbidden‑template protections). Scoring is binary: an unflagged candidate counts as a pass. The guarded pipeline permits at most one automated repair per pair; the repair operator is a constrained, localized edit routine limited to sequencing and small insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). Repair is applied only if the validator flags the shared_initial candidate and the repaired result is deterministically re‑validated.

Contamination and missingness controls. The preregistration included deterministic contamination detection (negative controls and invariant checks) and explicit exclusion rules: a pair would be excluded only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage. The missingness plan required logging provider errors and retaining pairs when only one call failed; in the confirmatory run no pairs were excluded.

Inferential procedures. The preregistered confirmatory analysis uses a paired contingency summary (n11,n10,n01,n00), an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10,000) to bound effect size. Preplanned sensitivity checks include failure‑as‑zero handling and stratum‑wise exploratory tests with multiplicity control.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The registered adapter completed the confirmatory run with 600 completed episodes yielding 300 complete pairs under the shared_initial protocol. Total model calls used was 301 (one repair stage invoked across the run). Deterministic reconciliation confirmed consistent episode accounting and no provider‑caused exclusions.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300 (baseline = 299/300 = 0.9966667; guarded = 300/300 = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts (n10,n01) returned p = 1.0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (seed = 1729, B = 10,000) is [0.00, 0.01]. With only one discordant pair, inferential sensitivity is limited; the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this experimental context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per stratum: low baseline = 100/100 & guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 & guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 & guarded = 100/100. The solitary discordant pair resided in the high stratum. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission (the shared_initial candidate lacked an explicit 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair operator performed one localized insertion; the repaired candidate then passed deterministic validation. The single deterministic rescue required one permitted repair invocation.

Contamination and missingness. Preplanned contamination checks and negative controls produced no unexpected pass behavior. No episodes were excluded and no provider outages occurred that affected confirmatory accounting.

Operational footprint. The guarded pipeline incurred minimal extra model‑call cost in this run: a single additional repair-stage call across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), showing low marginal cost for the observed deterministic rescue under the chosen repair operator.
sections.discussion:
Estimand conditioning and operational interpretation. The shared_initial estimand corresponds to operational policies that restrict model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons. Under this conditioning the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validation and bounded repair applied to the same generator output. Workflows that permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration change the estimand and typically achieve higher success rates by exploiting generator variance; such workflows should be evaluated under a different preregistered design.

Ceiling effects and the unexecuted pilot. The preregistration targeted a detectable absolute improvement substantially larger than the observed 0.00333; because the optional calibration pilot was not executed the main run confronted a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300), producing minimal discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute differences. This underscores the value of small pilots to estimate discordance when generator performance may approach ceiling on a chosen suite.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single rescued failure was a sequencing omission; richer failure classes (reachability, ACL semantics) were not observed at scale on this synthetic suite. The marginal utility of validator‑assisted rescue therefore depends on the real‑world distribution of failure modes and the validator's expressiveness. If operator policy forbids automated edits, the guarded pipeline's operational value shifts toward detection and human escalation.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to measure bounded deterministic rescue. Allowing iterative or more powerful repair operators, or enabling verifier‑guided regeneration, would likely increase rescue rates but addresses a different operational estimand and imposes higher model‑call costs. Our archived repair transcript enables forensic analysis to guide permissible edit‑operator design in production pipelines.

Practical implications. For organizations that enforce tight budgets on model calls, the shared_initial estimand provides an operationally relevant bound on deterministic verifier/repair rescue. Conversely, organizations willing to permit resampling or interactive steering should evaluate those alternative estimands directly, because they can materially increase success rates relative to single‑draw, bounded repairs.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study that conditioned on a single LLM draw per intent, a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair produced a single deterministic rescue among 300 pairs (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300). The absolute paired improvement was 0.00333 (exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.01]). Under the synthetic suite and the bounded repair budget the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We release preregistration, validator traces, repair transcript, task manifests, and analysis artifacts with the run bundle to support reproducibility and targeted follow‑ups that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task heterogeneity, or repair budgets.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated deterministically; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase the marginal utility of guarded pipelines.
Single model and validator: only the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and one deterministic validator were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended to estimate discordance and calibrate power was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative verifier‑guided regeneration).
Repair budget: guarded condition permitted at most one constrained automated edit per pair; iterative or more powerful repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
